content.description: Idli/dosa batter turns unpleasantly sour from fermenting too long.
content.symptoms: Strong sour smell and taste beyond the normal mild tang.
content.diagnosis: Left to ferment too long or in too warm an environment.
fixes: Use it for dosa (which tolerates more sourness) rather than idli
Add a pinch of baking soda to balance sourness
prevention: Refrigerate the batter once it has fermented enough

content.description: Ground chutney turns watery and separates instead of staying emulsified.
content.symptoms: Liquid pools on top after grinding or sitting.
content.diagnosis: Too much water added while grinding, or chutney sat too long before serving.
fixes: Grind with minimal water and adjust consistency at the end
Serve fresh
prevention: Add water gradually while grinding

content.description: Coconut/vegetable chutney develops an unexpected bitter edge.
content.symptoms: Bitterness noticeable despite normal ingredients.
content.diagnosis: Garlic or spices burnt during tempering, or the brown part of the coconut ground in.
fixes: Redo the tempering carefully at moderate heat
Scrape away the brown coconut skin before grinding
prevention: Temper on medium heat and watch closely
Use only the white coconut flesh

content.description: Lentils/dal remain firm even after extended cooking.
content.symptoms: Dal stays grainy/hard rather than turning creamy.
content.diagnosis: Old dal stock, hard water, or salt/acidic ingredients added too early.
fixes: Continue cooking with more water
Add a pinch of baking soda to help soften (use sparingly)
prevention: Add salt and tamarind/tomato only after the dal is fully cooked soft

content.description: Dosa turns out soft/chewy instead of thin and crisp.
content.symptoms: Dosa doesn't crisp at the edges even after cooking.
content.diagnosis: Batter too thick, too much rice flour vs. urad dal, or tawa not hot enough.
fixes: Thin the batter slightly with water
Cook on a hotter tawa
Spread the batter thinner
prevention: Get the rice-to-urad-dal ratio right
Preheat the tawa well before pouring batter

content.description: Dosa tears or sticks when trying to flip or remove it from the tawa.
content.symptoms: Batter clings to the pan surface instead of releasing cleanly.
content.diagnosis: Tawa not seasoned/heated properly, or too little oil.
fixes: Heat the tawa properly and season it with oil before the first dosa
Use enough oil around the edges
Let the dosa cook fully before attempting to lift it
prevention: Use a well-seasoned cast-iron or non-stick tawa
Maintain consistent medium heat

content.description: South Indian filter coffee tastes bitter/harsh instead of smooth.
content.symptoms: Sharp bitterness overwhelms the coffee-chicory flavour.
content.diagnosis: Over-extraction (too long a drip time or too fine a grind) or too high a coffee-to-water ratio.
fixes: Dilute with more hot milk
Use a coarser grind or reduce drip time next time
prevention: Follow the traditional slow-drip method for the right extraction

content.description: Stored ghee develops an off, rancid smell/taste.
content.symptoms: Ghee smells sour or 'off' rather than nutty and fresh.
content.diagnosis: Moisture contamination or prolonged exposure to heat/light.
fixes: Discard rancid ghee
prevention: Always use a completely dry spoon
Store in an airtight container away from direct heat/sunlight

content.description: Idli/dosa batter fails to rise after the usual fermentation period.
content.symptoms: Batter stays flat and smells the same as when mixed; no bubbles.
content.diagnosis: Ambient temperature too cold, too little urad dal, or old/dead fermenting culture (no starter batter).
fixes: Keep the batter in a warm spot (oven with light on, or near a warm appliance)
Increase the urad dal proportion slightly
Add a spoon of old fermented batter as a starter
prevention: Ferment in a warm season/location
Use fresh urad dal
Don't over-wash away the natural yeasts

content.description: After a full night the idli/dosa batter has not risen - it is the same volume, flat on top, with no bubbles or sour smell - and the idlis come out dense and hard.
content.symptoms: No rise; no domed surface; smells raw, not sour; heavy rubbery idli.
content.diagnosis: The batter was kept too cold, or not left long enough, or the salt was added in a large amount before fermenting, or the urad dal was old / poorly ground.
fixes: Move the batter somewhere warmer (near the stove, in the oven with just the light on, or wrapped in a towel) and give it several more hours.
Stir in a spoon of live batter or plain yoghurt as a starter and wait again.
If it still will not rise, add a pinch of baking soda just before steaming for that batch and grind a fresh batch of urad dal next time.
prevention: Ferment at 25-30 C; in a cold kitchen use the oven light or an instant-pot yoghurt setting.
Add most of the salt after fermentation, not before.
Use fresh urad dal and grind it light and fluffy; add a few fenugreek seeds when soaking.

root_causes: old or badly ground urad dal

content.description: Steamed idlis come out dense and hard instead of soft and spongy.
content.symptoms: Idli is compact, doesn't spring back when pressed.
content.diagnosis: Under-fermented batter, batter ground too coarse, or over-steaming.
fixes: Steam for the correct time only (usually 8-12 minutes)
Ensure batter is well-fermented and light before steaming
prevention: Grind batter to the right smooth-but-slightly-grainy consistency
Don't skip fermentation time

content.description: Papad doesn't puff up fully when fried or roasted.
content.symptoms: Papad stays flat or only partially expands.
content.diagnosis: Oil not hot enough (if frying) or papad too old/dried out.
fixes: Increase oil temperature and fry briefly
Use fresher papad
prevention: Store papad in an airtight container away from moisture

content.description: Milk-based payasam curdles/splits instead of staying smooth.
content.symptoms: Visible curdled specks in the payasam.
content.diagnosis: Adding an acidic ingredient (like fruit) to hot milk too quickly, or milk cooked at too high heat for too long.
fixes: Add acidic ingredients off the heat and gradually
Cook milk-based payasam on low-medium heat
prevention: Temper acidic additions in slowly at the end

content.description: Pickle develops mould during storage.
content.symptoms: Visible fuzzy growth on the surface or jar sides.
content.diagnosis: Insufficient oil/salt as a preservative, moisture contamination, or a non-dry serving spoon used.
fixes: Discard affected pickle
Remake with adequate oil/salt and ensure the jar and spoon are completely dry
prevention: Always use a dry spoon
Keep pickle submerged in oil
Store in a cool, dry place

labels: Pongal came out dry and stiff

content.description: The finished pongal is thick, stiff and sliceable instead of soft and creamy, and it firms up further as it cools.
content.symptoms: Holds sharp edges; hard to stir; pasty rather than creamy on the tongue.
content.diagnosis: Not enough cooking liquid, or the mixture was cooked/held too long after the water was absorbed.
fixes: Stir in hot water a little at a time over low heat until it loosens to a soft dropping consistency, then fold in a spoon of extra ghee.
Serve immediately; pongal always thickens on standing.
prevention: Use about 4.5-5 cups water per 1 cup rice-plus-dal.
Take it off the heat while it still looks slightly loose.

root_causes: fast pressure release drying the surface

content.description: Puttu turns out dry and falls apart instead of holding together lightly.
content.symptoms: Puttu crumbles excessively when unmoulded.
content.diagnosis: Rice flour not moistened enough before steaming.
fixes: Sprinkle and mix water into the flour until it just holds together when pressed, before steaming
prevention: Test the flour's moisture with a pinch-test before layering into the steamer

content.description: Puttu turns out soggy/gummy instead of light and fluffy.
content.symptoms: Puttu feels dense and sticky.
content.diagnosis: Too much water added to the rice flour before steaming.
fixes: Reduce the water slightly next time and steam a touch longer
prevention: Add water gradually, testing texture as you go

content.description: Rasam lacks the light frothy top that indicates it's properly finished.
content.symptoms: Rasam looks flat/thin on top instead of slightly frothy.
content.diagnosis: Boiled too vigorously for too long, or rasam powder added too early and cooked out.
fixes: Heat gently and remove from heat as soon as it just starts to froth, don't let it hard-boil
prevention: Add rasam powder near the end and avoid a rolling boil after

content.description: Rasam tastes overpoweringly sour rather than balanced.
content.symptoms: Sourness dominates over the pepper/tomato/spice notes.
content.diagnosis: Too much tamarind or tomato relative to water and spice.
fixes: Dilute with more water/dal water
Balance with a touch of jaggery
prevention: Measure tamarind extract carefully

content.description: Cooked rice turns out sticky/mushy instead of separate grains.
content.symptoms: Grains clump together and lose shape.
content.diagnosis: Too much water or overcooked.
fixes: Use the correct water-to-rice ratio for the variety
Reduce cooking time slightly
prevention: Rinse rice before cooking to remove excess surface starch

content.description: Rice grains remain hard/uncooked in the centre.
content.symptoms: Bite resistance is too firm, grains taste starchy-raw.
content.diagnosis: Too little water or insufficient cooking time.
fixes: Add a little more water and continue cooking covered
Extend cooking time
prevention: Measure water correctly for the rice variety used

content.description: Sambar lacks the expected tangy, spiced depth of flavour.
content.symptoms: Tastes flat despite having the right ingredients.
content.diagnosis: Too little tamarind/sambar powder, or tempering (tadka) skipped or added too early.
fixes: Adjust tamarind and sambar powder to taste
Add a fresh tempering of mustard seeds, curry leaves, and asafoetida just before serving
prevention: Always finish with a fresh, hot tempering

content.description: Sambar turns out thin and soup-like instead of a thick stew consistency.
content.symptoms: Sambar doesn't coat the back of a spoon.
content.diagnosis: Too much water added, or dal under-cooked/under-mashed.
fixes: Simmer uncovered to reduce and thicken
Mash the cooked dal well before adding vegetables
prevention: Measure water against dal quantity carefully

content.description: Ground spice powder (sambar/rasam podi etc.) loses its fragrance and potency over time.
content.symptoms: Powder smells and tastes flat compared to when freshly made.
content.diagnosis: Prolonged storage, exposure to air/light/moisture, or storing whole roasted spices ground too far in advance.
fixes: Use within a few weeks of grinding for best flavour
prevention: Store in an airtight container away from light and heat
Grind in smaller batches more frequently

content.description: Tempering (tadka) burns instead of sizzling and releasing aroma.
content.symptoms: Mustard seeds/curry leaves turn black and smell acrid rather than fragrant.
content.diagnosis: Oil too hot or tempering left in the pan too long.
fixes: Discard the burnt tempering and redo it at a slightly lower heat
prevention: Add ingredients to the tempering in the right order (mustard seeds first, curry leaves/asafoetida last) and keep heat moderate

content.description: Vadas turn out greasy/oily instead of crisp and light.
content.symptoms: Vada feels heavy and oil-soaked when bitten.
content.diagnosis: Oil not hot enough when frying, or batter too soft/wet.
fixes: Fry at the correct hot oil temperature (test with a small drop of batter)
Firm up the batter before shaping
prevention: Always test oil temperature before frying a full batch

content.description: Vada turns out dense/flat instead of having the characteristic airy holes.
content.symptoms: Vada lacks the light doughnut-like texture.
content.diagnosis: Batter over- or under-beaten, or not aerated enough before frying.
fixes: Beat the batter well to incorporate air before shaping
prevention: Beat until the batter feels light and slightly increases in volume
